title: Urea and electrolytes
subtitle: Sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine, eGFR and bicarbonate
summary: Sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine, eGFR and bicarbonate
introduction: Reference ranges shown are RVH (local) adult ranges. Interpret electrolytes with symptoms, fluid status, medication, urine output and previous results. Creatinine and eGFR must be interpreted against baseline; eGFR is unreliable during rapidly changing kidney function.

rows.name: Sodium
lowInterpretation: Hyponatraemia. Confirm chronicity and assess volume status, glucose, serum osmolality, medication, heart/liver/renal disease and SIADH causes.
highInterpretation: Usually free-water deficit from reduced intake or excess loss; less commonly sodium gain.

rows.name: Potassium
lowInterpretation: GI or renal losses, diuretics, insulin or intracellular shift. Can cause weakness and arrhythmia.
highInterpretation: AKI/CKD, ACE inhibitor or ARB, potassium-sparing diuretic, trimethoprim, tissue breakdown or acidosis. Exclude haemolysed sample where appropriate.

rows.name: Bicarbonate
lowInterpretation: Metabolic acidosis or respiratory alkalosis. Consider sepsis, renal failure, DKA, diarrhoea, lactate or toxins.
highInterpretation: Metabolic alkalosis or compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis; consider vomiting, diuretics or chronic hypercapnia.

rows.name: Urea
lowInterpretation: Low protein intake, liver dysfunction, pregnancy or excess fluid.
highInterpretation: Reduced renal clearance, dehydration, GI bleeding, catabolism, corticosteroids or high protein intake. Interpret beside creatinine.

rows.name: Creatinine
lowInterpretation: Often low muscle mass; usually not kidney failure.
highInterpretation: Reduced filtration, but assess change from baseline. AKI can occur with a creatinine still inside the stated reference range.

rows.name: eGFR
rows.referenceRange: calculated with the electrolyte profile; results above the reporting threshold are shown as >60 mL/min
lowInterpretation: May reflect CKD or AKI. CKD requires persistence for at least 3 months or another marker of kidney damage. Do not stage an acute change using eGFR alone.
highInterpretation: Usually reported as ≥90; a high estimate can be misleading in low muscle mass.

rows.name: Stage 1
rows.referenceRange: Rise ≥26 micromol/L within 48 h, or 1.5–1.9 × baseline within 7 days
highInterpretation: Treat as clinically important AKI and identify cause, medication risks, fluid status and complications.

rows.name: Stage 2
highInterpretation: More substantial AKI; usually requires urgent clinical assessment and close monitoring.

rows.name: Stage 3
rows.referenceRange: Creatinine ≥3 × baseline, or ≥354 micromol/L with acute rise ≥44 micromol/L, or renal replacement therapy
highInterpretation: Severe AKI requiring urgent hospital-level assessment.

calculations.title: AKI warning stage from creatinine
calculations.formula: Creatinine-based AKI warning stage using current/baseline ratio and a ≥26 µmol/L rise within 48 hours
interpretation: This calculator assesses creatinine criteria only. AKI can also be identified or staged using urine output; renal replacement therapy and the wider clinical context are not captured here.
Use a clinically appropriate recent baseline. The NHS AKI warning algorithm uses historical creatinine selection rules that are more sophisticated than a single manually entered baseline.

A positive warning stage requires urgent clinical interpretation: review the patient, fluid status, medicines, sepsis/obstruction risk and complications rather than treating the stage number in isolation.

parityCases.description: Current creatinine is 1.5 to less than 2 times baseline.
Current creatinine is 2 to less than 3 times baseline.
Current creatinine is at least 3 times baseline.
Current creatinine is at least 354 µmol/L and at least 1.5 times baseline.

inputs.label: Baseline creatinine
inputs.validationMessage: Enter baseline creatinine between 10 and 3000 µmol/L.

inputs.label: Current creatinine
inputs.validationMessage: Enter current creatinine between 10 and 3000 µmol/L.

inputs.label: Time between results
inputs.validationMessage: Use a baseline result from within the previous 7 days (0–168 hours).

urgentFindings: Potassium ≥6.0 mmol/L, rapidly rising potassium, ECG change, weakness, bradycardia or arrhythmia. Local thresholds may mandate emergency treatment at a lower result.
Sodium <125 mmol/L with confusion, seizure, reduced consciousness, severe headache or vomiting; or a rapid recent fall.
Sodium ≥160 mmol/L, neurological symptoms, marked dehydration or inability to access water.
AKI with oliguria (urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hour), pulmonary oedema (orthopnoea, bibasal crackles, hypoxia), hypotension, sepsis, severe acidosis or uraemic symptoms.
Creatinine rise ≥26 micromol/L within 48 hours or ≥50% above baseline within 7 days meets AKI criteria even if eGFR is still displayed.
overrides: Use the reporting laboratory’s reference ranges and compare with previous results, symptoms, observations, medication and fluid status.

commonPatterns.title: Pre-renal AKI / volume-depletion picture
findings: Urea raised proportionally more than creatinine (raised urea:creatinine ratio)
Creatinine rising but relatively preserved for the degree of illness
Clinical signs of dehydration or reduced oral intake
interpretation: Suggests renal hypoperfusion (pre-renal) rather than established intrinsic kidney injury
Often reversible with prompt correction of volume status
actions: Assess fluid status (skin turgor, mucous membranes, postural blood pressure, urine output)
Review for reversible causes: vomiting, diarrhoea, poor intake, diuretics, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs
Arrange same-day medical review if AKI staging criteria are met (see AKI detection section)

commonPatterns.title: AKI with hyperkalaemia
findings: Creatinine meeting AKI staging criteria (see AKI detection section)
Potassium above the normal range, particularly ≥6.0 mmol/L
interpretation: Combined AKI and hyperkalaemia is a time-critical combination — cardiac risk rises with both the potassium level and its rate of rise
ECG changes can lag behind the potassium result and may be absent even at dangerous levels
actions: Obtain a 12-lead ECG and look specifically for tented T waves, widened QRS, flattened P waves or arrhythmia
Treat as a time-critical presentation per local urgent/emergency escalation pathway
Do not wait for symptoms — hyperkalaemia can be asymptomatic until arrhythmia occurs

commonPatterns.title: Sick-day-rules trigger picture
findings: Rising urea and creatinine in a patient established on an ACE inhibitor, ARB, diuretic or NSAID
Intercurrent illness with vomiting, diarrhoea, fever or reduced oral intake
interpretation: Classic trigger for medicine-related AKI on a background of reduced renal reserve
Nephrotoxic or renally-cleared medicines can compound volume depletion from the acute illness
actions: Apply locally agreed sick-day-rules guidance: consider temporarily withholding relevant medicines during acute illness
Advise on oral rehydration where appropriate and safe
Safety-net for worsening symptoms and arrange follow-up U&E to confirm recovery

commonPatterns.title: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia (possible SIADH)
findings: Sodium below the normal range
Urea at the low end of or below the normal range
No clinical evidence of dehydration or fluid overload
interpretation: Raises the possibility of SIADH: consider medicines (e.g. SSRIs, carbamazepine, opioids), chest infection, CNS pathology and malignancy as causes
Distinguishing SIADH from other causes of hyponatraemia depends on accurate volume assessment, which can be difficult clinically
actions: Review the medication list for known causes of SIADH
Assess for chest and neurological symptoms/signs
Arrange same-day or urgent medical review for further work-up, particularly if sodium is <125 mmol/L or the patient is symptomatic (see urgent findings)

commonPatterns.title: Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia
findings: Sodium below the normal range
Urea raised, often with a raised urea:creatinine ratio
Clinical signs of dehydration or volume loss (vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretic use, poor intake)
interpretation: Sodium and water are both lost, but relatively more water is retained, producing dilutional hyponatraemia on a background of true volume depletion
actions: Assess fluid status and identify the source of fluid loss

Correct volume depletion cautiously — rapid correction of longstanding hyponatraemia carries a risk of osmotic demyelination, which is a reason for medical/senior input rather than unsupervised community correction

commonPatterns.title: Possible rhabdomyolysis picture
findings: Potassium raised
Creatinine raised disproportionately quickly relative to the clinical picture
History of a long lie, crush injury, seizure, extreme exertion or prolonged immobility
interpretation: Muscle breakdown releases potassium, myoglobin and creatine kinase, and can cause AKI
This picture is easy to miss if a long lie or reduced mobility is not specifically asked about
actions: Actively ask about a long lie, falls with an inability to get up, seizure or prolonged immobility
Request creatine kinase to confirm and quantify muscle injury (see further testing)
Treat as time-critical if hyperkalaemia or AKI meeting staging criteria (see AKI detection section) is also present, and encourage oral fluids where safe and appropriate

commonPatterns.title: Hypokalaemia (consider co-existing hypomagnesaemia)
findings: Potassium below the normal range
Diuretic use (particularly loop or thiazide), poor intake, vomiting or diarrhoea
interpretation: Magnesium deficiency commonly co-exists with, and can perpetuate, hypokalaemia — potassium may not correct until magnesium is also replaced
Can cause weakness and arrhythmia, particularly in patients on digoxin
actions: Review diuretic and other relevant medicines
Request magnesium alongside potassium replacement planning (see further testing)
Arrange ECG if the patient is symptomatic, or potassium is ≤3.0 mmol/L, or ≤2.5 mmol/L (RVH critical-result threshold)

commonPatterns.title: Thiazide-induced hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia
findings: Sodium below the normal range
Potassium below the normal range
Current thiazide or thiazide-like diuretic (e.g. bendroflumethiazide, indapamide)
interpretation: A well-recognised combination, more common in older adults and often within days to weeks of starting or increasing the dose
Distinct from the SIADH and hypovolaemic hyponatraemia patterns above — medication is the primary driver here
actions: Review whether the thiazide is still indicated and discuss with the prescriber
Arrange medical review, particularly if sodium is <125 mmol/L or the patient is symptomatic (see urgent findings)

commonPatterns.title: Isolated hyperkalaemia with normal renal function
findings: Potassium above the normal range
Urea, creatinine and eGFR within normal limits
No AKI-related history or examination findings
interpretation: Consider a haemolysed or delayed sample, difficult venepuncture, or a fist-clenching/tourniquet artefact before treating as a true result
Also consider drug causes (ACE inhibitor/ARB, potassium-sparing diuretic, trimethoprim, NSAIDs) and, rarely, adrenal insufficiency
actions: Correlate with the ECG — a normal ECG does not exclude true hyperkalaemia but supports reviewing the sample
Consider a repeat sample taken without a prolonged tourniquet time before escalating on the result alone
Do not dismiss a genuinely elevated result as artefact without a clear reason to suspect one

rationale: Gives a rapid bicarbonate, pH and lactate when the U&E bicarbonate is abnormal or the patient is unwell, without waiting for the full laboratory panel
Lactate helps identify hypoperfusion or sepsis as a driver of AKI
Helps identify infection, bleeding or haemolysis as a contributing or causative factor in AKI or an electrolyte disturbance
Supports assessment of an infective or inflammatory driver of AKI, particularly when sepsis is a differential
Confirms and quantifies muscle injury when rhabdomyolysis is suspected (e.g. long lie, seizure, crush injury, or hyperkalaemia with a disproportionate creatinine rise)
Hypomagnesaemia can cause refractory hypokalaemia and should be considered when potassium is difficult to correct
Deranged calcium and phosphate are relevant in AKI meeting staging criteria and in rhabdomyolysis

A single result can be misleading — the trend over serial results is often more clinically useful than one isolated value, particularly for borderline AKI staging or monitoring after a medicine change
Confirms whether an abnormal result is improving, stable or worsening before deciding on conveyance/escalation
Quick, immediately available in the community and can identify infection, haematuria or proteinuria as a contributing cause of AKI
Useful alongside urine output when assessing volume status and renal impairment
Quick to check on scene; relevant when bicarbonate is low, as DKA/HHS are differentials for a metabolic acidosis or dehydration picture, particularly in known diabetics
